questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects

questions.exp: C = constipation. (Book p123)

questions.q: In the muSCARINE mnemonic, the letter A stands for:

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: The example quoted for opioid-induced increased muscle rigidity is wooden chest syndrome with:
questions.exp: The page quotes 'wooden chest syndrome in Fentanyl' as the example of increased muscle rigidity. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: A patient on an intravenous fentanyl infusion suddenly develops a rigid chest wall that cannot be ventilated. This is an example of:
opts: Increased muscle rigidity - wooden chest syndrome
questions.exp: Wooden chest syndrome due to increased muscle rigidity is the classic example given for fentanyl. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: Pin-point pupils seen in opioid overdose reflect which mu receptor effect?
questions.exp: Miosis is the M of the muSCARINE mnemonic and produces the pin-point pupil of opioid overdose. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: Inability to pass urine after morphine is explained by which mu effect?
questions.exp: Urine retention (U of the mnemonic) is a mu receptor effect. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: The mu receptor effect on bile flow is:
questions.exp: The mu list includes reduced bile flow, which follows contraction of the sphincter of Oddi. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: The reduced bile flow produced by mu agonists is attributable to contraction of the:
questions.exp: The side note against the mu column reads 'contraction of sphincter of Oddi', which cuts bile flow. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: According to the mu receptor column, circular smooth muscle:
questions.exp: The mu column ends with 'circular smooth muscles: contract'. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: According to the mu receptor column, longitudinal smooth muscle:
questions.exp: The mu column ends with 'longitudinal smooth muscles: relax'. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a mu receptor effect?
questions.exp: Psychomimetic (dysphoria) is listed under the kappa receptor, not under mu. (Book p123)

questions.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
questions.q: The combination of contracted circular muscle and relaxed longitudinal muscle in the gut of a patient on morphine best explains:
opts: Constipation and spasm with reduced propulsive movement
Loss of the gastro-colic reflex only
questions.exp: Circular muscle contracts while longitudinal muscle relaxes, so non-propulsive segmental tone rises - the basis of opioid constipation. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: Constipation is listed as an effect of which receptors?
questions.exp: Constipation appears in the mu list (C of muSCARINE) and at the top of the kappa list. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: Analgesia is listed as an effect of:
questions.exp: Analgesia appears in all three receptor columns - mu, kappa and delta. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: The psychomimetic (dysphoria) effect of opioids is attributed to the:
questions.exp: Psychomimetic (dysphoria) is listed in the kappa column. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: Anti-pruritic action is a listed effect of the:
questions.exp: The kappa column lists anti-pruritus. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: Modulation of the release of neurotransmitters and hormones is listed under:
questions.exp: The delta column lists 'modulate release of: i. neurotransmitters, ii. hormones'. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: The two categories of release said to be modulated by the delta receptor are:
questions.exp: The delta column lists i. neurotransmitters and ii. hormones. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: A patient on an opioid complains of dysphoria and strange dreams while still having good pain relief. The receptor most responsible is:
questions.exp: Psychomimetic effects such as dysphoria are kappa mediated. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: Which receptor effect listed on the page is unique to the delta receptor?
opts: Modulation of neurotransmitter and hormone release
questions.exp: Only the delta column lists modulation of neurotransmitter and hormone release. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: According to the note on the page, opioids in biliary colic are:
opts: Not contraindicated because the analgesic effect exceeds the contraction
Absolutely contraindicated because they contract the sphincter of Oddi
Replaced by papaverine in all cases
questions.exp: The note reads 'Opioids not c/l in biliary colic (Analgesic effect > Contraction)'. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: The reasoning given for continuing opioids in biliary colic is that the:
opts: Analgesic effect is greater than the sphincter contraction
Biliary tree has no opioid receptors
Drug is excreted entirely in bile
questions.exp: The note justifies opioid use by stating analgesic effect > contraction. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: Difelikefalin is described as a:
questions.exp: The page states 'Difelikefalin: kappa agonist'. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: Difelikefalin is used for:
opts: Pruritus in CKD patients on dialysis
questions.exp: Difelikefalin is used for pruritus in CKD patients on dialysis. (Book p123)

questions.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
questions.q: A dialysis-dependent patient with refractory uraemic pruritus is best treated, per this page, with:
questions.exp: Difelikefalin, a kappa agonist, is the drug named for pruritus in dialysis patients. (Book p123)

Enkephalin - mu, endorphin - delta, dynorphin - kappa
Enkephalin - kappa, endorphin - mu, dynorphin - delta
Enkephalin - delta, endorphin - kappa, dynorphin - mu

units.title: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects
units.sec: Opioid Receptors and the mu (mu) Receptor Effects · p123
units.guide: The chapter opens with the three opioid receptors - mu, kappa and delta - and their effects. The mu effects are remembered by the mnemonic mMuSCARINE: miosis, urine retention, sedation, constipation, analgesia, respiratory depression and increased muscle rigidity (classically the wooden chest syndrome of fentanyl), followed by reduced bile flow from sphincter of Oddi contraction, contraction of circular smooth muscle and relaxation of longitudinal smooth muscle.

units.title: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin
units.sec: kappa and delta Receptor Effects, the Biliary Colic Note and Difelikefalin · p123
units.guide: The kappa receptor adds constipation, analgesia, anti-pruritic action and psychomimetic dysphoria, whereas the delta receptor produces analgesia and modulates the release of neurotransmitters and hormones. The page carries two clinical notes: opioids are not contraindicated in biliary colic because the analgesic effect outweighs sphincter contraction, and difelikefalin, a kappa agonist, is used for pruritus in dialysis-dependent CKD patients.

units.title: Endogenous Opioids
units.guide: The drug section begins with the endogenous opioids, which are synthesised within the body: enkephalin acting on the delta receptor, endorphin on the mu receptor and dynorphin on the kappa receptor.

units.title: Exogenous Opioids: Natural Opiates
units.guide: Exogenous opioids are first classified by source into natural opiates, semi-synthetic and synthetic drugs. Natural opiates are derived from Papaver somniferum and split into chemicals with opioid action (morphine and codeine) and chemicals without opioid action (noscapine, used as an anti-tussive for spasmodic cough; papaverine, which inhibits phosphodiesterase, raises cyclic AMP and relaxes smooth muscle in biliary and ureteric colic; and thebaine).

units.title: Semi-synthetic and Synthetic Opioids
units.guide: Semi-synthetic opioids are those derived from morphine (diacetylmorphine/heroin, four times as potent as morphine and a drug of abuse; apomorphine, a dopamine agonist used in Parkinson's disease; hydromorphone, ethylmorphine and the non-opioid anti-tussive pholcodine), from codeine (hydrocodone, an analgesic) and from thebaine (buprenorphine, oxycodone and oxymorphone). The synthetic group lists fentanyl, pethidine, loperamide and methadone.

units.title: Classification Based on Opioid Receptor Interaction
units.sec: Classification Based on Opioid Receptor Interaction · p124
units.guide: The second classification is based on opioid receptor interaction. Agonists are either full agonists or mixed agonist-antagonists, while antagonists are pure antagonists, which are further divided into central and peripheral agents.

units.title: Pure Centrally Acting Antagonists: Naloxone
units.sec: Pure Centrally Acting Antagonists: Naloxone · p125
units.guide: Pure centrally acting antagonists can cross the blood-brain barrier and are the drugs used in opioid toxicity. Naloxone is the shortest acting, is given intravenously (and intranasally in acute toxicity), is the drug of choice in opioid toxicity, and is used off label for valproate-induced CNS depression and clonidine toxicity; its adverse effects - hypertension, arrhythmias and pulmonary edema - follow the surge of catecholamines.

units.title: Nalmifene and Naltrexone
units.guide: Nalmifene is the long-acting antagonist, while naltrexone is the longest acting and is given orally. Naltrexone is the drug of choice in alcohol dependence and is used in opioid dependence to prevent relapse; its problems are hepatotoxicity (AST/ALT rising to three times normal, or frank liver failure) and dysphoria or depression from mu antagonism, which contraindicates its use.

units.title: Mixed Agonist/Antagonists: Nalorphine, Dezocine, Pentazocine and Butorphanol
units.sec: Mixed Agonist/Antagonists: Nalorphine, Dezocine, Pentazocine and Butorphanol · p126
units.guide: The mixed agonist/antagonist table lists the drug, its receptor interaction at mu, kappa and delta, and details. Nalorphine (earlier used in opioid toxicity, with fewer side effects because of mu antagonism, but a poor analgesic) and dezocine are mu antagonists with full kappa agonism, whereas pentazocine and butorphanol are mu partial agonists with full kappa agonism. Pentazocine raises heart rate and is contraindicated in a patient with myocardial infarction.

units.title: Eluxadoline, Buprenorphine and the Ceiling Effect
units.sec: Eluxadoline, Buprenorphine and the Ceiling Effect · p126
units.guide: Eluxadoline is a full agonist at mu and kappa and an antagonist at delta, used in irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at mu and an antagonist at kappa; because it binds fast and dissociates slowly (high affinity for mu) it produces no or only mild withdrawal symptoms and is used in opioid toxicity and, thanks to its ceiling effect, in mild to moderate pain. It is contraindicated in labour pain because it may cause naloxone-resistant respiratory depression in the fetus.
